title: Signature Petition Seed
body:
The Signature Petition Seed is Manon's original design for the smallest complete petition: one decision-maker, one action, one frozen ask, and one method of collection, written on a single page before anything else is done. The Seed's discipline is that nothing is collected until the Seed is complete, because a petition that starts collecting before its ask is frozen, its target is confirmed, and its rules are read will collect signatures that cannot be counted. The Seed page carries the ask in one sentence, the decision-maker's name, the receiving body's rules in plain words, the eligibility conditions, and the collection method, and it is signed and dated by the organizer as the petition's founding record. Later pages, collectors, and counts all refer back to the Seed, so any question about what supporters signed can be answered from one page.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-line seed design. First, the ask is written in one sentence, naming decision-maker, action, and scope. Second, the decision-maker's power to grant the ask is confirmed, in writing from the body's rules where possible. Third, the eligibility conditions are written in plain words on the Seed itself. Fourth, the collection method, paper or online, is chosen and its form prepared. Fifth, the Seed is dated and frozen, and any later change to the ask starts a new Seed and a new collection, rather than quietly altering the old one. The demo below checks a small seed for its five lines and names the missing one, which is the completeness check before collection begins.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature petition seed. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: seed lines complete: 4 of 5; missing line: ['rules read'] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when starting any petition, as its founding page. Do not use it as legal advice about petition rules in any jurisdiction, because rules differ and the receiving body's current rules govern. Do not use it to claim a petition guarantees an outcome, because most petition systems guarantee consideration or a response, not the action requested. title: Signature Ask Stone
body:
The Signature Ask Stone is Manon's original design for a petition ask that, once frozen, cannot be quietly changed. The Stone is a single page carrying the ask in one sentence, carved in the design's language, meaning written, dated, and stored where collectors and signers can see it, with any later version treated as a new Stone, not an edit to the old one. The design answers the most common petition drafting failure, which is an ask that drifts during collection, as organizers add clauses, soften language, or merge two asks, leaving early signers endorsing words that no longer exist. With the Stone, drift is visible: there is an old Stone and a new Stone, with different dates and different signature batches, and nobody can pretend they are the same petition.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part stone design. First, the ask is written in one sentence, naming decision-maker, action, and scope, and tested on three strangers for understanding. Second, the Stone is dated and stored with the petition's founding record, and copies given to collectors carry the same date. Third, collection begins only after the Stone is set, and collectors are briefed that the Stone does not change. Fourth, if the ask must change, a new Stone is set with a new date, and collection restarts under it, with the old batch kept separate and never merged into the new one. The demo below compares two stones by date and ask, which is the comparison that prevents accidental merging.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature ask stone. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 2026-10-01 - council repairs library roof; 2026-11-01 - council repairs library roof and extends hours; stones are different petitions - do not merge their batches Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when drafting any petition, and in collector training. Do not use it as legal advice about what a particular body can or must do, because powers differ by jurisdiction and body. Do not use it to merge batches collected under different asks, because merged batches misrepresent what supporters signed. title: Signature Wording Sieve
body:
The Signature Wording Sieve is Manon's original design for a four-mesh screen through which every petition sentence passes before publication. The first mesh catches unsourced factual claims, which must be sourced or removed. The second mesh catches opinions presented as facts, which must be labeled as opinions. The third mesh catches statements about named individuals that cannot be substantiated, which must be removed. The fourth mesh catches promises about the petition's effect that overstate what the rules guarantee, which must be rewritten honestly. A sentence that passes all four meshes is publishable; a sentence caught by any mesh is fixed, not published with a hope that nobody notices. The Sieve is used by the drafter and checked by a second reader, because drafters are blind to their own overstatements, and a second pair of eyes is the cheapest quality control a petition has.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-mesh sieve design. First, the background statement is read sentence by sentence, and each sentence is passed through the four meshes in order. Second, caught sentences are fixed at once: sourced, labeled, removed, or rewritten, with the fix noted. Third, the second reader runs the sieve independently and compares results, because two sieves catch more than one. Fourth, the sieved text is frozen with the ask, so later edits must pass the sieve again. The demo below screens three sentences by mesh result, which is the screen a drafter and a second reader run together.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature wording sieve. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: library closed 40 days last year -> passes - sourced; council does not care -> caught - opinion, label it; manager stole funds -> caught - unsubstantiated, remove; sentences caught: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when drafting or reviewing petition wording. Do not use it as legal advice about defamation or petition law, which differ by jurisdiction; organizers facing a risky claim should seek qualified advice. Do not use it to sanitize a petition into vagueness, because precision and honesty strengthen a petition, while vagueness weakens it. title: Signature Eligibility Gate
body:
The Signature Eligibility Gate is Manon's original design for a checkpoint at the point of signing that admits only eligible signatures. The Gate is a single question, asked before any signature is accepted, in the petition's own plain words, such as are you a resident of this area and aged eighteen or over, with the answer determining whether the signature is taken at all. The Gate's discipline is that eligibility is checked before signing, not after collection, because a signature collected from an ineligible signer cannot be fixed later, and a batch full of such signatures wastes the collection effort and damages the petition's credibility. The Gate is printed on every form, spoken by every collector, and built into every online form as a question that must be answered before the signature field appears.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part gate design. First, the eligibility conditions are extracted from the receiving body's rules in plain words. Second, the conditions are turned into one question, or a short set of questions, that a signer can answer honestly in seconds. Third, the question is placed before the signature, on paper and online alike, so no signature can be given before the gate is passed. Fourth, collectors are trained to ask the question neutrally, without suggesting the answer, and to decline politely where the answer is no, thanking the person and explaining why. The demo below sorts a small set of would-be signers through an example gate, which is the sorting collectors do at every signing.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature eligibility gate. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: resident, adult -> gate passes; visitor, adult -> gate stops - thank and explain; resident, under age -> gate stops - thank and explain; signatures admitted: 1 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for any petition collection, and in collector training. Do not use it as a statement of the rules for any particular petition, because eligibility rules differ by body and jurisdiction, and the receiving body's current rules govern. Do not use it to collect personal data beyond what the rules require, because signer privacy matters, and excess data creates risk without adding count. title: Signature Paper Sheet
body:
The Signature Paper Sheet is Manon's original design for a paper petition form that cannot be misread, misfiled, or misunderstood. The Sheet carries the ask at the top of every page, the eligibility conditions in plain words, one row per signer with exactly the fields the rules require, and a page number and petition identifier on every page, so no page can be mixed with another petition's pages and no signature can be collected on a page whose ask the signer did not see. The Sheet's rows are wide enough for legible handwriting, its fields are labeled in plain words rather than abbreviations, and its footer carries the collector's name and the collection date, so any question about a page can be answered from the page itself. The design's promise is that a well-designed sheet prevents the errors that validators later punish, because most invalidity is designed in at the form stage, not caused by signers.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part sheet design. First, the ask and eligibility are printed on every page, not only the first. Second, one row per signer is provided, with the required fields labeled plainly. Third, the page number and petition identifier are printed on every page. Fourth, collectors check each row at the point of collection, while the signer is present and can correct it. Fifth, completed pages are numbered, stored in order, and counted as collection proceeds, with the running eligible estimate kept separate from the raw count. The demo below checks a small batch of sheet rows for completeness, which is the check collectors run on the spot.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature paper sheet. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: name + signature + address -> complete; signature only -> incomplete - correct with signer present; name + signature + address -> complete; complete rows: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design for any paper petition collection, and in collector training. Do not use it to accept signatures on someone else's behalf, to pre-fill rows, or to alter entries after signing, because each of those can invalidate signatures and damage credibility. Do not use it to collect more personal data than the rules require. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

title: Signature Digital Sheet
body:
The Signature Digital Sheet is Manon's original design for an online petition form that behaves like a good paper sheet: it states the ask and eligibility plainly, it asks the eligibility question before the signature field appears, it collects exactly the fields the rules require, and it screens for duplicates as signatures arrive, rather than presenting an inflated count. The Sheet's discipline is that online ease must not become online sloppiness: a form that accepts any entry, from anyone, without checks, will produce a count that no receiving body trusts, while a form with a gate, a duplicate screen, and a plain data statement will produce a count that can be defended. The Sheet also states its data handling plainly to signers, before they sign, including what is collected, who holds it, and whether signers will be contacted afterwards, and it honors that statement exactly.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part digital sheet design. First, the receiving body's acceptance of the chosen platform or portal is confirmed before launch, because a platform petition and a formal petition are different things. Second, the form is built with the eligibility gate first, the required fields only, and a duplicate screen that runs continuously. Third, signatures are monitored as they arrive for duplicates, ineligible entries, and suspicious patterns, and flagged entries are handled promptly rather than presented as valid. Fourth, the data statement is written in plain words, shown before signing, and honored after submission. The demo below screens a small batch of online signatures for duplicates, which is the screen the Sheet runs continuously.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature digital sheet. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: ana@example.org -> new; ben@example.org -> new; ana@example.org -> duplicate; unique signatures: 2 of 3 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when planning any online petition. Do not use it as a recommendation of any platform, because no vendor is named or endorsed here, and platform terms change. Do not use it to present an online signature count as a verified count, because online counts are raw counts until the receiving body verifies them. title: Signature Validation Screen
body:
The Signature Validation Screen is Manon's original design for an organizer-side screen that predicts, before submission, what a receiving body's validation will find. The Screen has five meshes, matching the usual validation checks: completeness of required fields, eligibility of the signer, duplication across the whole petition, authenticity, meaning the signature was made by the signer named, and register match where the body checks one. The organizer runs the Screen on the full batch before submission, counts the survivors, and plans the submission message around the screened count, not the raw count, because the screened count is the honest estimate of the verified count, and the gap between a claimed count and a verified count is remembered long after the petition itself. The Screen's rule is that validation loss is normal, expected, and planned for with a margin, never a surprise that derails submission.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-mesh screen design. First, the batch is assembled in order, pages numbered and counted, so the Screen can trace any signature to its page. Second, each signature passes the five meshes in order, and failures are recorded by reason, so the organizer learns which collection problem to fix. Third, the screened count is computed and compared with any threshold, and a shortfall found here triggers more collection, not a hope that validators will be lenient. Fourth, the screening method and its results are recorded in the petition's log, so the submission message can state them honestly. The demo below applies a small screen to a batch and counts the survivors, which is the arithmetic organizers do before submission.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature validation screen. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: raw count: 4; screened count: 2; screened out: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when planning and running any petition, and in pre-submission review. Do not use it as a statement of any particular body's validation method, because methods differ, and the receiving body's current rules govern. Do not use it to dispute a validation result without evidence, because disputes need specific, checkable claims about specific signatures. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

title: Signature Invalidity Sorter
body:
The Signature Invalidity Sorter is Manon's original design for a sorting board that classifies every screened-out signature by its reason, so the organizer fixes the collection problem rather than merely lamenting the loss. The Sorter's five bins are incompleteness, illegibility, ineligibility, duplication, and authenticity, and every screened-out signature goes into exactly one bin, with the bin counts tallied after each collection phase. The bins teach different lessons: a full incompleteness bin means collectors need retraining on required fields, a full illegibility bin means the form needs wider rows or clearer labels, a full ineligibility bin means the gate is not being asked, a full duplication bin means the duplicate screen is not running, and any authenticity bin entry means a collector needs immediate attention. A sorter that shows where loss comes from is worth more than a count that only shows how much was lost.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-bin sorter design. First, the bins are labeled and defined in collector training, with one example per bin. Second, every screened-out signature is placed in exactly one bin at screening time, never left unclassified. Third, bin counts are tallied after each collection phase and reviewed at check-ins, so a growing bin triggers a fix before the next phase. Fourth, fixes are recorded against their bins, so the next tally shows whether the fix worked. The demo below tallies a small batch by bin, which is the tally organizers review at check-ins.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature invalidity sorter. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: incomplete: 2; illegible: 1; ineligible: 1; duplicate: 2; authenticity: 0; screened out total: 6 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design in collector training and pre-submission review. Do not use it to alter entries after signing in order to fix them, because alteration after signing can itself invalidate a signature; the remedy is to re-collect correctly. Do not use it to accuse any signer of dishonesty on the basis of a bin alone, because most invalidity is error, not dishonesty. title: Signature Circulation Map
body:
The Signature Circulation Map is Manon's original design for a map of where a petition will be circulated, marked by permission status before any collection begins. The Map lists every planned place, marks each as cleared, permission required and granted, permission required and pending, or not permitted, and assigns collectors to cleared places only, so no collector ever improvises a permission decision on the spot. The Map also carries the conduct rules for every place: honest identification, plain statement of ask and eligibility, no pressure, no misleading claims, no signing for others, and leaving when asked. The Map's discipline is that permission is confirmed before collection, not assumed during it, because a petition collected in a place where it was not welcome loses legitimacy even where its signatures are technically valid, and a map that shows where collection is welcome is a plan that collectors can actually follow.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part map design. First, the planned places are listed and, for each, permission is confirmed from the place's owner or manager, and the result is marked on the Map. Second, collectors are assigned only to cleared places, with the Map carried as their authorization. Third, collectors are briefed on the conduct rules and equipped with the petition, the eligibility wording, and a contact for questions. Fourth, a circulation log is kept, recording where, when, and by whom each batch was collected, so any question about a batch can be answered from the log. The demo below lists a small map by permission status, which is the map organizers complete before their first collection day.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature circulation map. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: public square -> cleared; shopping center -> permission granted; private office -> permission pending; places cleared: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when planning petition circulation, and in collector training. Do not use it as legal advice about where petitioning is permitted, because rules differ by jurisdiction, place, and owner, and permission should be confirmed for each place. Do not use it to collect in a place after permission has been refused, because refusal ends the matter for that place. title: Signature Count Board
body:
The Signature Count Board is Manon's original design for a visible board that keeps a petition's three numbers honest and separate: the raw count, the screened count, and the verified count. The board shows all three numbers side by side, with the screening method stated beneath them, and it is updated at every collection check-in, so supporters, collectors, and decision-makers always see the same numbers, and nobody mistakes a raw count for a verified one. The board's rule is that the verified count, once known, becomes the petition's public figure, and earlier figures are kept visible as history, not hidden, because a petition that shows its counting honestly is trusted even when its verified count is lower than hoped, while a petition that hid its screening is distrusted even when its count is high.

Method. The working method for this record is a three-number board design. First, raw signatures are counted by page and by collector, and page totals are reconciled to the grand total. Second, the organizer's screening is applied, with deductions recorded by reason, producing the screened count. Third, the verified count, once the receiving body confirms it, is added to the board, and the board's history is kept, showing how each number was reached. Fourth, every public statement about the petition uses the board's current honest figure for its stage: raw during collection with its screening note, screened before submission, verified after validation. title: Signature Submission Parcel
body:
The Signature Submission Parcel is Manon's original design for a submission package that cannot be lost, questioned, or confused with another petition. The Parcel contains the petition in the required order, with pages numbered and counted; a cover sheet naming the petition, its ask, its organizer contact, and its three-number count; a complete copy of everything submitted, kept by the organizer; and a receipt sleeve, holding the acknowledgment the receiving body gives, naming the petition, the count submitted, and the date. The Parcel's discipline is that submission is not complete when the petition is handed over, but when the receipt is in the sleeve and the copy is filed, because the copy and the receipt are the organizer's protection if the original is questioned, lost, or disputed. A petition submitted without a copy and without a receipt is a petition the organizer cannot prove they submitted.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part parcel design. First, the receiving office, form, format, deadline, and cover requirements are confirmed in writing well before the deadline. Second, the petition is assembled in the required order, numbered, counted, and copied completely. Third, the Parcel is submitted by the required method, and the receipt or acknowledgment is obtained and placed in the sleeve, with follow-up if none arrives within the body's stated time. Fourth, the submission is recorded in the petition's log, and supporters are informed that submission has happened, with the submitted count stated honestly. The demo below checks a small parcel checklist, which is the checklist organizers run on submission day.

Do not use it as a statement of any particular body's submission rules, because rules differ, and the receiving body's current rules govern. Do not use it to submit after a deadline in the hope of leniency, because deadlines in formal petition systems are often strict. title: Signature Jurisdiction Compass
body:
The Signature Jurisdiction Compass is Manon's original design for a comparison tool that points a petition at the right body and level before collection begins. The Compass has four needles, one per question: which body decides, at which level, under which rules, and with what response promise? The organizer turns each needle by reading the body's official rules, and the Compass points to a single target, because a petition designed for two levels at once usually satisfies neither. The Compass also records its sources, so any later question about why this target was chosen can be answered from the record. The design's insight is that jurisdiction is not a detail to be checked after collection but the first decision a petition makes, because every later choice, from eligibility to format to deadline, flows from it, and a petition aimed at the wrong body fails however many signatures it collects.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-needle compass design. First, the decision-maker and its level are identified precisely, because similar-sounding bodies at different levels have different rules. Second, the body's current petition rules are obtained from its official source, and the threshold, eligibility, format, deadline, and response promise are extracted in plain words. Third, the rules are compared across any levels the petition might target, and one target is chosen and recorded with its source. Fourth, collection, validation, and submission are designed around the chosen body's rules, and the Compass record is kept in the petition's log. The demo below compares three example levels by threshold and response, which is the comparison the Compass displays.

Do not use it to assume that a method valid in one jurisdiction is valid in another, because that assumption is the most common cross-jurisdiction error. title: Signature Timeline Wheel
body:
The Signature Timeline Wheel is Manon's original design for a petition timeline drawn as a wheel, with the submission deadline at its hub and the phases radiating outward in reverse order, so the organizer sees at a glance how much time each phase has and what happens if one slips. The wheel's phases are drafting and freezing the ask, printing or building the collection form, collection itself, screening and deduplication, assembling and copying the submission, and submission, with a margin phase before submission for corrections. The wheel is drawn before the first collection day, with owners named for each phase and check-ins marked during collection, at which the raw count, the screened count, and the remaining time are reviewed together, so a shortfall is found early enough to fix. The wheel's rule is that screening and assembly are never compressed to rescue a late collection, because a rushed submission is where catchable errors become permanent.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-phase wheel design. First, the submission deadline is fixed from the body's rules and placed at the hub, with its counting method noted. Second, the phases are laid out backwards from the hub, with dates and owners, and a margin phase before submission. Third, check-ins are marked during collection, where counts and time are reviewed together. Fourth, post-submission communication is planned on the wheel's outer ring: what supporters will be told, when, and by whom, during validation and while awaiting a response. The demo below lists a small wheel's phases and counts them, which is the plan organizers write before their first collection day.

Do not use it as a guarantee that a timeline will hold, because collection rates vary and margins exist for that reason. Do not use it to compress screening or assembly to rescue a late collection, because a rushed submission is where errors that could have been caught become permanent. title: Signature Second Attempt
body:
The Signature Second Attempt is Manon's original design for a disciplined response to a rejected petition, structured so the second attempt fixes the first attempt's actual cause rather than repeating it. The design begins with the rejection reasons in writing, in full, classified into five classes: form, count, wrong body, out of powers, or negative answer, each with its own remedy: correct and resubmit, re-run with better collection and a larger margin, redirect to the right body, redesign the ask, or continue advocacy. The Second Attempt is planned with the same discipline as the first, including its margin and screening, and it is never an unchanged resubmission, because repeated identical submissions waste the body's time and the petition's credibility. The design's promise is that a rejection, handled this way, becomes a diagnosis, and a diagnosis becomes a better petition, rather than a wasted effort.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-step second-attempt design. First, the rejection reasons are obtained in writing, recorded with dates and the body's reference, and shared honestly with supporters. Second, the rejection is classified into one of the five classes, because each class has a different remedy. Third, the remedy that fits the class is chosen and planned, with a new timeline, margin, and screening method. Fourth, the second attempt is run with the same discipline as the first, and its result is compared with the first attempt's, so the organizer learns whether the fix worked. The demo below classifies three example rejections by remedy, which is the classification organizers make before acting.

Use and limits. Use this design after any petition rejection, and in civic education. Do not use it as legal advice about challenging a rejection, because appeal rights differ by jurisdiction and body, and organizers considering a challenge should seek qualified advice. Do not use it to resubmit an unchanged petition repeatedly, because repeated identical submissions waste the body's time and the petition's credibility. title: Signature Signer Vault
body:
The Signature Signer Vault is Manon's original design for a secure, minimal store for petition signer data. The Vault's rules are minimize, state, secure, and close: collect only the fields the rules require, state plainly to signers what is collected, who holds it, who sees it, and how long it is kept, store paper forms locked with limited access and online data access-limited under a named holder, and handle the data after submission exactly as the rules and the statement require, deleting or returning what should not be retained. The Vault is deliberately boring: it has one holder, one key or access list, one log of who opened it and when, and no other features, because a vault with extra features is a vault with extra ways in. Signer lists are never shared, sold, or published beyond what the rules and the signers' consent allow, and signers are never contacted for unrelated purposes on the basis of a signature.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-rule vault design. First, minimize: the Vault accepts only the fields the rules require, and any extra field is refused at intake. Second, state: the Vault's statement to signers is written in plain words on the form, before signing, and honored exactly. Third, secure: the Vault has one named holder, limited access, and a log of openings, for paper and online alike. Fourth, close: after submission, the Vault's contents are handled as the rules and the statement require, the handling is confirmed to signers where promised, and data that should not be retained is deleted or returned. The demo below checks a small vault routine by status, which is the check organizers run before their first collection day.

Use and limits. Use this design when planning any petition collection, and in collector training. Do not use it as legal advice about data protection law, which differs by jurisdiction and turns on specific facts. Do not use it to publish signer lists or contact signers for unrelated purposes, because either breaks the trust the petition depends on. title: Signature Petition Plan
body:
The Signature Petition Plan is Manon's original design for a two-page plan covering the petition facet only: the frozen ask, the target body and its rules, the eligibility conditions, the collection places and collectors, the timeline with its phases and owners, the screening and counting method, and the submission routine with its receipt step. The Plan is written before collection, reviewed at each collection check-in, and kept as the petition's log, so any later question about the petition, from validators, decision-makers, or supporters, can be answered from it. The Plan deliberately excludes the wider organizing campaign, such as building a coalition or running public events, which belongs to the companion organizing basics database, because a plan that tries to cover everything covers nothing well, and the petition's strength is that it is a countable, verifiable instrument aimed at one decision-maker, not a symbol of a cause.

Method. The working method for this record is a six-part plan design. First, the frozen ask and the target body and its rules, with their official source, are recorded. Second, the collection method, places, and collectors are listed, with permissions confirmed. Third, the timeline is written with phases, owners, and check-ins. Fourth, the screening, deduplication, and counting method is written, with the three numbers it will produce. Fifth, the submission routine is written, including the copy and receipt steps. Sixth, the plan is reviewed at each check-in, updating counts and dates but never changing the frozen ask without restarting collection under the new wording. The demo below lists a small plan's sections by status, which is the completeness check organizers run before their first collection day.

Use and limits. Use this design when planning any petition, and in civic education. Do not use it as a substitute for the companion organizing basics database, which covers building support, coalitions, and campaigns around a cause. Do not use it to change the ask mid-collection without consequence, because changing the ask can invalidate earlier signatures under some rules.
